title: Roof coverings and rainwater goods for the Prairie Avenue 1904 programme (package K04, the library)
status: Built to since T-2293: the 1808 Prairie exemplar (data/structures/keith_house_1808_prairie.json, generators/archetypes/k01_frontage.py) is slated in slate_pennsylvania with copper_sheet caps, valleys, apron, step flashing, gutter and pipes, every one of its dimensions read from the profiles below through generators/archetypes/k01_frontage_params.py (docs/RESEARCH/k04-1808-roof-2293/README.md).
rule: A fabric's module is DATA, here, and the map is generated from it: every coursed map's tile is a whole number of its own slates, tiles, pans or sheets (tile_m = columns x width, courses x exposure), so a K01 roof that maps TEXCOORD_0 = surface metres / tile_m registers its courses at true size and no slate is ever scaled to fit a roof. Edges, caps, valleys, aprons, gutters and pipes are GEOMETRY built from the profiles below, never painted into a covering map.

slots._doc: The K01 roof family's material_slots, and which fabrics may fill each. covering is the roof plane; flashing every valley, apron, step and cap; rainwater the gutters, outlets, pipes and shoes (a K04 addition: the K01 contract's roof family names covering, flashing, fascia and soffit, and rainwater goods hang below its eave socket).

defaults._doc: What a house gets when its own record says nothing better. A default is a reconstruction (confidence reconstructed), and a house whose photograph or drawing shows its covering takes that instead.

steep_main_roof.note: The study's register describes slate on every steep main roof whose covering it names (pa-1912-10 Moulton/Lowden, pa-2100-18 Sherman, pa-1801-23 Kimball; slate mansards at pa-2115-19 Kelley/Armour and pa-1900-25 Keith). Dark Pennsylvania slate is the working default; the register's readings are the study's, not source records here.

mansard_lower_face.note: The register's 'patterned slate mansard' (pa-2115-19): a coloured field with scalloped bands. Which bands, how many and in what colours is house-specific and is never repeated from one mansard to the next.

low_slope_service_roof.note: Bounded low-slope service roofs over rear ranges, porches and kitchens: soldered flat-seam tin, painted, which sheds water at a pitch slate cannot.

porch_and_bay_roof.note: Porch, bay and dormer-cheek roofs between the service roof's pitch and slate's.

oriel_and_tower_cap.note: The register's copper oriel caps (pa-2110-30 Rees, pa-213-217-e.-cullerton-street-27, the 1880s copper bay at pa-2018-s.-calumet-avenue-31). Its warning stands: modern patina is not proof of the 1904 state, so the fabric is brown, not green.

documented_on.locator: p. 21: tiles about 6 in wide with 5 in exposed

restrictions.why: ASSET-CATALOG.md section K04: 'documented terracotta tile only where supported'. Tile is never a default, and no house wears it without a source of its own here.
Scalloped slate is an accent: bands on a mansard, a tower cone, a dormer. A whole main roof of it is a choice a house's own evidence has to make.
Copper on oriel caps, bay roofs and tower caps; a whole main roof of copper is not this district's working default.

fabrics.rule_source: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Slate courses (0.20-0.30 m width, 0.15-0.25 m exposure)
fabrics.note: A 10 x 20 in slate on a 3 in headlap, so 8.5 in to the weather: exposure = (length - headlap) / 2, the double-lap rule. Blue-black to dark grey, near-uniform, with the faint lengthwise cleavage grain of a riven slate and a few slates a shade off. Size, lap and colour are reconstructed.

fabrics.rule_source: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Slate courses
fabrics.note: A 9 x 18 in slate on a 3 in headlap, 7.5 in to the weather. A grey-green field with sea-green slates weathering towards buff and a sparse purple: the colour mix of a coloured or patterned roof, dealt per slate from a smooth field so no two neighbours repeat and nothing reads as a checkerboard. Size, lap and mix are reconstructed.

fabrics.rule_source: RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md section Starting ranges: Slate courses
fabrics.note: An 8 x 16 in slate dressed to a full semicircular butt (radius half the slate's width), 6.5 in to the weather on a 3 in headlap, in the dark Pennsylvania colour. For bands, cones and dormers (restrictions). Format and colour are reconstructed.

INFERRED module, RECONSTRUCTED appearance. The 6 in width and 5 in exposure are HABS's (data p. 21, 1963) for Glessner, carried to 1904; the tile's length and lap follow from the exposure on the double-lap rule. The red of unglazed fired clay, its grain and the per-tile variation are ours. documented_only (restrictions).

20 in pans between double-locked seams 1 in high, with a flat-locked cross seam every 8 ft staggered half a sheet from the next pan. Copper some years in the weather: brown to dark brown with faint downslope streaks, not the green the register warns is modern. Pan width, seam and colour are reconstructed.

Terne (tin-coated iron) in 20 x 28 in sheets joined end to end with a flat cross seam every 28 in, run in 20 in pans between standing seams, painted red oxide. Sheet size, seam and paint are reconstructed; the paint is one of the alternatives listed, and a house's own evidence picks another.
Terne in 14 x 20 in sheets, edges folded into half-inch flat locks, soldered, laid in broken joint and painted: the low-slope service roof. Sheet size, lock and paint are reconstructed.
Plain dressed copper for valleys, aprons, caps, ridge rolls, gutters and pipes: brown, with the soft undulation of hand-dressed sheet. A plain fabric: its folds and edges are geometry.
Dull grey lead, the soft metal dressed over chimney steps and stone copings, with bossing marks. A plain fabric; folds are geometry.
Pale blue-grey weathered zinc (or galvanized iron), for flashings, gutters and pipes. A plain fabric; folds are geometry.
Painted terne flashing and rainwater goods, in the paint of the tin roofs beside it. A plain fabric; folds are geometry.

profiles._doc: Engine-neutral parameters for the parts K04 builds as GEOMETRY (ASSET-CATALOG.md section K04: slate exposure/lap; cut edges; hip/ridge caps; valley flashing; dormer apron; gutter bracket; downpipe shoe). Metres. Every value is reconstructed: a working design inside period practice, replaceable by a house's own drawing or photograph.

headlap_m.below_25: not slated: use a seamed metal covering

slate_exposure.starter_course: a doubled eave course with its slates laid lengthwise-cut so every joint is broken
slate_exposure.note: The double-lap rule: every point of the roof is covered by two thicknesses of slate and the headlap is the third. A steeper roof sheds faster and takes the smaller lap.

hip.note: Slates cut on the hip line and mitred, with no slate narrower than 75 mm at the hip (a narrower piece is a half-and-half: two slates cut together).

verge.note: Slate-and-a-half at alternate courses so the verge never ends in a narrow piece.

dressing.note: The butt and sides dressed from the back, leaving a narrow broken bevel on the face; the covering maps carry it at map scale and the cut edges carry it at the hip.

slate_saddle.note: Two slates meeting at the ridge, one combing over the other, for a plain slate roof.

copper_ridge_roll.note: A rolled copper cap on wood, flanges dressed down over the top courses: the K01 roof's flashing slot.

terracotta_ridge.note: Glessner's raised tile crest is the canonical asset's own, not K04's (T-2016, T-2157).

valley_flashing.note: An open metal valley that widens downhill, with a crimped centre rib, slates cut to the line on both sides. Never a zipper of overlapping slates.

dormer_apron.note: The apron dressed over the course below the dormer's face, step flashings at its cheeks one per course with counter-flashing over them.

chimney_flashing.note: A cricket on the uphill side of any stack wider than 0.75 m (RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md: chimneys pierce roofs with flashing).

built_in_box.note: Lined into the cornice behind its crown moulding, the masonry house's usual eave; no hung gutter shows.

bracket.note: Wrought iron hangers on the fascia or the first course's sheathing, at 30 in.

outlet.note: One outlet per 12 m of eave at most, each over a downpipe.

downpipe.note: Every gutter outlet leads to a pipe and every pipe ends AT GROUND: a shoe kicked out over a splash stone, or a boot into the drain (RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md: gutters lead to downpipes; T-1846 acceptance: drainage ends at actual ground).
